passages.original: Sed jam vel nunc accipiat, cbarissime frater, qui te minime audire detractat, sanctum atque egregium praedicatorem antistitem Augustinum : et licet pene in omnibus opusculis suis, ubi eum causa exegit, animam vel angelum instruat incorporeum , verumtamen quia angustia temporis (sicut jam diximus) coarctat, libros ejus nec vobis transmittere, nec nobis legere vacat, pauca etiam quae nobis ex libris ejus ad incorporalitatem animae aut angeli astruendam in mentem veniunt, scribere curavimus.
passages.english: But now at least, dearest brother, let him who refuses to listen to you at all accept the holy and distinguished preacher, the bishop Augustine. And although in almost all his works, wherever the subject required it, he establishes that the soul or an angel is incorporeal, nevertheless, since the shortness of time (as we have already said) constrains us, and there is leisure neither to send his books to you nor for us to read them, we have taken care to write down at least the few things from his books that come to mind for establishing the incorporeality of the soul or of an angel.
passages.notes: "cbarissime" read as "charissime" (scanning error). "instruat" is taken in the sense "establishes" (cf. "astruendam"); possibly a corruption of "astruat".

passages.original: In libro etiam de Origine aimæ,quem ad sanctum Hieronymum presbyterum scripsit , incorpoream quoque esse animam inquit: etsi difficile tardioribus persuaderi potest, mihi tamen fateor esse persuasum. Haec verba beati Augustini ostendunt illos non posse Intelligere animae incorporalitatem , qui ingenio pusillo non valent sejungere corporea ab incorporeis rebus : quia scilicet tantum corporis sensibus dediti, nihil esse existimant quod non per sensus corporis percepisse meminerint.
passages.english: Also in the book On the Origin of the Soul, which he wrote to the holy presbyter Jerome, he says that the soul is also incorporeal: "even if this can hardly be made convincing to slower minds, I confess that I myself am convinced of it." These words of blessed Augustine show that those who, with their small intelligence, are unable to separate corporeal things from incorporeal ones cannot understand the incorporeality of the soul: for, being devoted only to the senses of the body, they think that nothing exists which they do not remember having perceived through the bodily senses.
passages.notes: "aimæ" read as "animae" (scanning error). The work meant is Augustine's letter to Jerome on the origin of the soul (Letter 166). The extent of the quotation is not marked in the text; quotation marks are supplied around the clause that appears to be Augustine's words.
